title: Thesis Literature Gap Finder
problem: Graduate students drafting a thesis or dissertation lit review often summarize what's already been studied but struggle to sharply articulate the specific, defensible gap their own work fills. The most common advisor feedback — 'so what hasn't been done, and why does that matter?' — usually means the gap was described too vaguely to defend.

workflow.step: 1. Map the field, not just your topic
workflow.detail: Ask the model to organize your source notes into the sub-questions the field has already answered, before talking about your own project at all.
Run the Prompt Template with your mapped sub-questions and proposed methodology to get candidate gap statements.
For every candidate, ask 'has anyone actually done this?' and go verify against the real literature yourself — models are prone to confidently declaring a gap that's already been published.
Bring the sharpened gap statement to your advisor before writing the full review around it. This is a supervision checkpoint, not a step to skip.

workflow.step: 5. Write the review argued toward the gap
workflow.detail: Regenerate the literature review section using the confirmed gap as the throughline, rather than as a neutral, undirected survey.

promptTemplate:
Help me identify a defensible research gap for a thesis in {{FIELD}}.

WHAT THE FIELD HAS ALREADY ESTABLISHED (from my source notes):
{{ESTABLISHED_FINDINGS}}

MY PROPOSED METHODOLOGY / ANGLE:
{{METHODOLOGY}}

1. Organize the established findings into the sub-questions the field has already answered.
2. Identify 2-3 candidate gaps — specific, narrow claims about what hasn't been addressed — that my proposed methodology could plausibly fill.
3. For each candidate gap, state exactly what evidence would be needed to prove it's a real gap (not already covered), so I can go verify it myself.

variables.name: ESTABLISHED_FINDINGS
variables.label: Established findings (from your source notes)
variables.placeholder:
Remote work reduces burnout for high-autonomy roles (Lee, 2022)...
Hybrid schedules show mixed effects on team cohesion (Osei, 2023)...

variables.name: METHODOLOGY
variables.label: Your proposed methodology / angle
variables.placeholder: e.g. Longitudinal survey of low-autonomy manufacturing roles moved to hybrid schedules

exampleOutput:
**Sub-questions already answered:** (1) Does remote work reduce burnout in high-autonomy roles? (2) What are hybrid schedules' effects on team cohesion?

**Candidate gap:** Existing burnout research concentrates on high-autonomy knowledge work; low-autonomy roles moved to hybrid schedules are largely unstudied.

**To verify this is real:** Search for any longitudinal study of hybrid/remote transitions specifically in low-autonomy or manufacturing-adjacent roles published in the last 5 years — if none exists, the gap holds.
tips: Never accept a model's claimed gap without checking it yourself — 'no one has studied X' is exactly the kind of claim LLMs confidently get wrong.
Bring the sharpened gap statement to your advisor before writing the full review — a wrong gap caught after a full draft costs weeks; caught before costs one meeting.
Long-context models (Gemini, Claude) handle Step 1 well if you paste in dozens of source notes at once — save smaller/faster models for the iterative gap-wording passes.
A gap stated as a question ('has X been studied in Y context?') is easier to verify than one stated as a claim ('no one has studied X') — prefer the question form.
